title: What Is the Cost of Manual KYB Workflows?
summary: Manual KYB cost covers analyst time, rework, lost onboardings, missed owners, and later audit reconstruction. Corporate reviews average $2,274.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** The cost of a manual KYB workflow is the analyst's hour plus the work that hour creates: a second pass through the file, a customer who leaves, an ownership chain that stops too early, and a decision that has to be rebuilt for an exam. Fenergo's 2024 survey of 453 bank executives in the UK, the US, and Singapore put the average KYC review for a corporate or commercial client at $2,274. A fintech will not match that large-bank figure, and it will still pay the same five costs.


## The Hour on the Timesheet Is the Smallest Number


A manual KYB workflow is the work a firm does before it will bank, pay, or platform a legal entity. Someone confirms the entity exists, collects documents, identifies the people who own or control it, screens those people, and writes down why the file was cleared.[Business verification](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/what-is-kyb-complete-guide-to-know-your-business) is that whole sequence, not a single registry lookup.


[Fenergo's 2024 research report](https://fincrime.news.blog/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/kyc-trends-2024-banking-report-final.pdf) , based on a Censuswide survey of 453 C-suite executives at banks in the UK, the US, and Singapore, put the average cost of a KYC review for a corporate or commercial client in multiple jurisdictions at $2,274. That was down 12% from a 2023 average of $2,598. Respondents ran banks with more than $50 billion in assets, surveyed in September 2024. A fintech with simpler entities will not match the dollar amount.


The same report put the average time to complete a KYC review at 90 days in 2024, down from 95 days in 2023. US banks moved the other way, from 82 days in 2023 to 90 days in 2024. Over half of the US firms in that survey, 54%, still run 70% of corporate client onboarding by hand.


## Five Costs Inside One File


Finance usually sees one line: analyst time. The file produces four more. Rework, delayed onboarding, a missed owner, and the reconstruction an examiner triggers later each have their own unit. Price them separately, or the hourly rate will keep looking cheaper than the workflow actually is.


Cost What it looks like in the file What to count


Analyst time Registry checks, documents, screening, and the written conclusion Fully loaded minutes, split by simple and multi-entity files


Rework A second request, a re-keyed field, a name that did not match Share of files opened twice before a decision


Delayed onboarding Days between a complete application and a decision Days open, and applicants who leave


Missed owners A chain that stops at a holding company, or no control person Approved files missing either prong


Audit reconstruction A conclusion that lives in email or with someone who has left Hours to reproduce a closed file


### Analyst time


[1LoD's 2025 Financial Crime Benchmarking Survey](https://fincrime.news.blog/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/the-2025-financial-crime-benchmarking-survey-and-report-a-1lod-survey.pdf) covered more than 25 Tier 1 and Tier 2 firms in the US, Europe, and Asia. 94% of those banks named high manual workload as the key operating challenge in AML and KYC. For 60% of them, more than half of AML and KYC processes still depend on manual intervention. The tasks inside that share are ordinary: a registry extract that disagrees with the application, a document someone has to read, a screening hit on a common name, and a narrative someone has to type.


### Rework


Fenergo found that 93% of the banks in its survey named manual processing and data management as the main barrier to efficiency, and 84% named siloed data and weak communication between the front, middle, and back office. Silos create the second request. The certificate of incorporation arrives, sits in a queue the onboarding analyst cannot see, and the customer is asked for it again. The registration number is already on the application and still gets typed into a second system.


### Delayed onboarding


Two-thirds of the banks Fenergo surveyed in the UK, the US, and Singapore, 67%, said they had lost a client in 2024 because onboarding was slow and inefficient. In the prior year's study, 48% of global firms reported losing clients because of onboarding. That revenue does not post to the compliance cost center. The customer never starts, and the analyst time already spent on the abandoned file stays on the books.


A payments applicant who waits three weeks for an ownership question can finish somewhere else.[Speeding up business verification](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-speed-up-business-verification-processes) is its own operating problem. The cost question is what those idle days are worth once the applicant is gone and the first review has already been paid for.


### Missed owners


[FinCEN's CDD Rule](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/cdd-rule-faqs) defines a beneficial owner as each individual who, directly or indirectly, owns 25% or more of the equity interests of a legal entity customer, and one individual with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct that customer. Under that definition a legal entity has between one and five beneficial owners: one control person, and zero to four people on the ownership prong. A file that stops at a holding company has not finished the work. When nobody owns 25%, the control person is still required.


The expensive version of this miss is an approval. A Delaware holding company owns the operating subsidiary, and the holding company's member is a person. The analyst clears the subsidiary, screens the registered agent, and never identifies the member.[Mapping ownership through holding companies](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/ubo-mapping-automation) closes that gap while the file is fresh. Collecting below the 25% line is permitted. A file with no control person is unfinished.


### Audit reconstruction


Identifying information, including the certification form or its equivalent, has to be kept for five years after the account is closed. Verification records have to be kept for five years after the record is made. FinCEN's FAQs also require a description of every document relied on, the non-documentary methods used, and the resolution of any substantive discrepancy. A note that says the registry was checked does not meet that bar.


An examiner who samples accounts opened two years earlier will find the certification in the core system and the reason a name mismatch was accepted in a mailbox belonging to someone who has left. Rebuilding that sample is a project the firm bought at onboarding.


## The 2026 Relief Shrinks Repeat Collection


On February 13, 2026, FinCEN issued an exceptive relief order under 31 CFR 1010.230(b). A covered institution that uses the relief does not have to identify and verify beneficial owners every time an existing legal entity customer opens another account. Collection can be limited to the first account, to any later point where the institution knows facts that reasonably call the earlier information into question, and to whatever its risk-based ongoing customer due diligence requires. An institution can still collect at every new account if it chooses.


The order can shrink collection on a second product when ownership has not changed. The first file stays, and so does the refresh, which is where a stale chart usually surfaces. Ongoing customer due diligence remains an AML program requirement: understand the relationship, monitor for suspicious activity, and update customer information on a risk basis. The FAQs, updated on May 6, 2026, fold the relief into the existing rule.


[FATF's March 2023 guidance](https://www.fatf-gafi.org/en/publications/Fatfrecommendations/Guidance-Beneficial-Ownership-Legal-Persons.html) on Recommendation 24 tells countries to keep beneficial ownership information adequate, accurate, and up to date, and to combine sources so a single registry entry is not the only check. A manual team that treats the first clean extract as the answer is building a file the standard will not accept. The second source, and a note on whether the two sources agreed, is part of a file that can be defended.


## How to Price the Workflow You Already Run


Price the workflow you already run: files, minutes per file, and the loaded rate.


A cost model for manual KYB starts from closed files, not from a salary divided by a target number of onboardings. Pull a recent sample of entity decisions, including declines and stalls, and score each file on six measures.


A vendor price only means something beside that baseline. A tool that only relocates the re-key leaves second touches, incomplete ownership prongs, and reproduction hours unchanged.[Reducing compliance cost](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/how-to-reduce-compliance-costs-in-fintech) across a fintech is a wider problem than entity onboarding. A[KYB automation shortlist](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/best-kyb-automation-platforms-fintech-2026) is a buying decision that comes after the baseline exists, and the buying question is which of the six measures the tool actually moves.


## Where Sphinx fits


Sphinx's agents take the repetitive middle of a KYB file inside the systems analysts already use. They pull the entity, walk the ownership chain, screen the people the chain produces, and write the decision down as the work happens. That write-up is the record the five-year retention rule expects, produced when the decision is made. Across production casework, Sphinx has cut case review time by 80%, and 98% of cases are resolved the same day. A KYB program still has to measure its own minutes, second touches, and lost applicants against that baseline.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What does a manual KYB review cost?


The closest published benchmark is Fenergo's 2024 figure: $2,274 on average to complete a KYC review for a corporate or commercial client in multiple jurisdictions, down 12% from $2,598 in 2023. The survey covered large banks in the UK, the US, and Singapore, so a fintech with simpler entities will not match the dollar amount. The shape of the cost is the same: analyst time, a second pass, days the customer waits, and a file that has to be explainable later.


### Why is analyst time the smaller part of KYB cost?


The hour shows up on a timesheet. The rest of the cost is the file sitting open, the customer who does not finish, and the reconstruction when an examiner asks how the ownership conclusion was reached. Fenergo found that 67% of surveyed banks in the UK, the US, and Singapore had lost a client to slow and inefficient onboarding in 2024, and that loss never lands on a timesheet.


### Did FinCEN's 2026 exceptive relief reduce KYB work?


The February 13, 2026 order lets a covered institution skip a fresh beneficial-ownership collection on later accounts for the same legal entity, when the first collection is still reliable and ongoing due diligence does not call for an update. The first account, any sign that the earlier information is unreliable, and risk-based ongoing monitoring still require the work. Repeat-account collection can shrink, and the opening file stays the same size.


### How long does a firm have to keep a KYB file?


Under the CDD Rule, identifying information, including the certification or an equivalent, must be kept for five years after the account closes. Verification records must be kept for five years after the record is made, including the documents relied on and how any substantive discrepancy was resolved. A workflow that cannot retrieve those records without rebuilding them from email pays the retention cost twice.


### What should a team measure before automating KYB?


Measure minutes per file, the share of files touched twice, calendar days to a decision, applicants who drop, approved files missing an ownership prong or a control person, and the hours required to reproduce a closed file. Those six numbers are the cost of the current workflow. A vendor price only means something next to them.
